The theory of sets is a hugely important basis for many other areas of mathematics, with a long history.

Definition 1.1 - Set

A set is a collection of objects. The objects belonging to a set are called elements or members of the set. We might define the elements in a set by giving a list, or stating a property they all share. A set has no duplicates, and the order of the objects in the set is not important.S = \{ a, b, c \} \qquad \mathbb{N} = \{ 1,2,3,4 \ldots\} \qquad X = \{ x \in \mathbb{N}: 1 \leq x \leq 10 \}

Sets are usually denoted by capital letters and set elements are denoted by lower case letters.
The symbol \in is used to denote ‘is an element of’ or ‘belongs to’ or ‘a member of’.

We need sets to be well-defined, which means it should always be possible from the definition of a set to decide whether a given element belongs to the set or not.

The elements of a set can be written in a list, separated by commas, in between a pair of set brackets: \{ \}.

Theorem 1.1 - The Axiom of Extensionality

Two sets A and B are equal if and only if A and B contain the same elements.

A set is completely defined by its elements

The order the elements are listed in the set is irrelevant

If the same element is listed more than once, the additional instances can be ignoredS = \{ a, b, c \} = \{ a, c, b \} = \{ a, b, b, c, c,c,c,c \}

We can write a set by specifying the underlying set its elements are drawn from, then giving a condition the elements must meet in order to be included in the set.X = \{ x \in \mathbb{N}: 1 \leq x < 6 \} = \{ 1,2,3,4,5\}

Here X is the set we are defining, and its elements are drawn from the natural numbers \mathbb{N}. In order to be included in this set, a natural number x must satisfy \leq x < 6. The number 6 is not strictly less than itself, so it is not included in the set.Y = \{ x \in \mathbb{N}: x = 2k, k \in \mathbb{N} \} = \{ 2, 4, 6, 8, \ldots\}

The condition can involve other variables, as long as they are also well-defined.Z = \{ x \in \mathbb{N}: x \textrm{ has exactly two prime factors} \} = \{ 4, 6, 9, 10, 14, 15, \ldots\}

If the condition cannot easily be expressed using algebra, it can instead be stated in words.

Note

When reading this notation aloud, the colon : separating the underlying set from the condition can be read as ‘such that’. A vertical line | is sometimes used in place of the colon.

## Some well-known sets

- **The natural numbers, $\mathbb{N}$**

A natural number is a positive whole number .
$$ \mathbb{N} = \{ 1,2,3,4, \ldots \} = \{ x\ |\ x \textrm{ is a natural number }\}$$

Note: some definitions of $\mathbb{N}$ include zero; it can be useful to clarify which you mean. We use the term 'positive integers' to mean $\{1,2,3, \ldots \}$ and 'non-negative integers' or sometimes 'whole numbers' to mean $\{0,1,2,3, \ldots\}$ (which is also occasionally denoted $\mathbb{N}_0$).

- **The integers, $\mathbb{Z}$**

The integers are the positive and negative whole numbers, including zero:

$$ \mathbb{Z} = \{ \ldots, -3, -2, -1, 0, 1, 2, 3, \ldots \} =  = \{ x\ |\ x \textrm{ is an integer }\}$$

We can also define the positive and negative integers:

$$ \mathbb{Z}^+ = \mathbb{N} = \{ 1, 2, 3, \ldots \} \qquad \mathbb{Z}^- =\{ -1, -2, -3, \ldots \}$$

- **The rational numbers, $\mathbb{Q}$**

A rational number is a ratio of two integers in the form $\frac{p}{q}$ where $q \neq 0$.

$$ \mathbb{Q} = \{ x | x = \frac{p}{q}, p,q \in \mathbb{Z}, q\neq 0\} = \{ x | x \textrm{ is a rational number}\}$$

- **The irrational numbers, $\mathbb{Q}'$**

An irrational number is a real number which cannot be written as a ratio of two integers $\frac{p}{q}$.

$$ \mathbb{Q}' = \mathbb{R}\setminus \mathbb{Q}= \{ x | x \neq \frac{p}{q}, p,q \in \mathbb{Z}\} = \{ x | x \textrm{ is an irrational number}\}$$

- **The real numbers, $\mathbb{R}$**

Real numbers are the collection of all rational and irrational numbers.

$$\mathbb{R} = \mathbb{Q} \cup \mathbb{Q}' = \{ x | -\infty < x < \infty \} = \{ x | x \textrm{ is a real number}\}$$

We can also define the positive and negative real numbers:

$$ \mathbb{R}^+ = \{ x \in \mathbb{R} | x > 0\} \qquad \mathbb{R}^- =\{  x \in \mathbb{R} | x < 0\}$$

- **The complex numbers, $\mathbb{C}$**

Complex numbers are numbers of the form $z =a + ib$ where $a$ and $b$ are real numbers and $i$ is the imaginary unit $\sqrt{-1}$.

$$\mathbb{R} = \{ z = a +ib | a,b \in \mathbb{R} \} = \{ z | z \textrm{ is a complex number}\}$$

## Intervals

Many useful examples of sets can be defined as sections of $\mathbb{R} - usually, the set of numbers between a pair of given endpoints.

```{admonition} Definition 1.2 - Interval
:label: interval-definition

An **interval** of the real line is a finite section of $\mathbb{R}$ defined in terms of its endpoints. Intervals can be open or closed, depending on whether they include or exclude their endpoints.

- Closed interval: $[a,b] = \{ x \in \mathbb{R} | a \leq x \leq b \}$
- Open interval: $(a,b) = \{ x \in \mathbb{R} | a < x < b \}$
- Half-open interval: $[a,b) = \{ x \in \mathbb{R} | a \leq x < b \} \textrm{ or } (a,b] = \{ x \in \mathbb{R} | a < x \leq b \}$

A square bracket at an endpoint indicates it is included in the set, whereas a parenthesis (round bracket) indicates it is
not included.

Definition 1.3 - Subset

A subset is a set whose elements are contained in a larger set. We say A is a subset of B, denoted A \subseteq B, if every element of A is also an element in B.A \subseteq B \Leftrightarrow x \in A \Rightarrow x \in B \Leftrightarrow B \supseteq A

We can also say that B is a superset of A.

If A is not a subset of B - that is, there is at least one element of A which does not belong to B - then we write A \not\subseteq B.

A proper subset is a subset which is not equal to the larger set - we write A \subset B, or say ‘A is properly contained in B’, if there is at least one element of B not in A.A \subset B \Leftrightarrow x \in A \Rightarrow x \in B, A \neq B

Note

This notation follows the same rule as the <, >, \leq, \geq symbols we use for ‘less than’ versus ‘less than or equal to’, etc. The second line under the symbol mimics the = symbol.

For example,

P = \{x\}, T = \{x, y, z\} and M = \{v, w, x, y, z\} are all subsets of L = \{v, w, x, y, z\}, and P and T are proper subsets. Therefore, we may write P \subset L, T\subset L and M\subseteq L.

S_1 = \{1,2,3\} and S_2 = \{1,2\}. Then S_2 \subseteq S_1 but S_1 \not\subset S_2.

\mathbb{N} \subset \mathbb{Z}, since every natural number is also an integer. Also, \mathbb{Z} \subset \mathbb{Q}, since every integer number is also a rational number (e.g. 3 = \frac{3}{1}), and \mathbb{Q}
\subset \mathbb{R}$, since every rational number is also a real number.

:label: properties-of-subsets-theorem
:class: attention

- For any set $A$, we have $A \subseteq A$.
- If $A \subseteq B$ and $B \subseteq C$, then $A \subseteq C$.

Definition 1.4 - The universal set

The universal set, denoted by U, is a set containing all  is a set containing all the elements of all sets under consideration. For example, if we are working with sets of real numbers, U = \mathbb{R}.

If we are studying human populations, the universal set consists of all the people in the world.

In plane geometry, the universal set consists of all points in the plane.

We could define U to be the set of whole numbers from 1 to 10 (i.e. U=\{1, 2, 3, \cdots
9, 10\}), and then only consider sets which are subsets of U.

Definition 1.5 - The empty set

The empty set, sometimes also called the null set, is a set containing no elements. It can be denoted by \{\} or \varnothing.

For example,\{x | x \in \mathbb{N}, x < 0\} = \varnothing

Definition 1.6 - Unit set

A unit set is a set containing only a single element. For example, S = \{x\}.

Note

Note that x, the element, is distinct from \{x\}, the set containing only the element x. To denote a unit set, we write S = \{x\}, not S = x.

Theorem 1.2 - Properties of the universal and empty sets

\varnothing is a subset of every set A, and a proper subset of every set A \neq \varnothing.

For any set A, we have \varnothing \subseteq A \subseteq U.

Definition 1.7 - Set equality

Two sets A and B are equal (denoted A=B), if and only if they have exactly the same elements. That is, each member of A is a member of B, and vice versa.A = B \Leftrightarrow A \subseteq B, B \subseteq A

Definition 1.9 - Set difference

The relative complement of a set B with respect to a set A or, simply, the difference of A
and B, denoted by A\B, is the set of elements which belong to A but which do not belong
to B; that is 𝐴\𝐵 = {𝑥|𝑥 ∈ 𝐴, 𝑥 ∉ 𝐵}
The set A\B is read “A minus B” many texts denote 𝐴\𝐵by 𝐴 − 𝐵.
